label: Night Signal
tagline: A warning told in glowing pictograms on black, with the threat in red.

messages.mascot: Mascots are not available in the Night Signal style: its pictogram scenes keep one red threat as the only coloured figure, and a mascot would break that. Choose another visual style, or no mascot.

review:
- This video is a Night Signal warning, and the following are its intended, approved look: a near-black field with lots of empty black; flat warm-white pictograms (round heads with no faces, rounded bodies, simple objects) with a soft glow, standing on one thin ground line; exactly one red thing in a scene, the threat, sometimes a faceless red figure whose head is blurred; a case-file row near the top with a FILE number, a short title, a row of small squares and a running timecode; a doorbell-camera panel with a blinking REC dot and a clock; a phone screen; a RULE card with a red prohibition ring and slash; a case card with grey redaction bars; a navy card of numbered steps; faint scanlines, grain and a dark vignette over everything; scenes changing through two to four frames of torn, colour-split horizontal slices; captions in spaced white capitals. Do NOT report any of these as defects, and do not suggest colour, photographs, faces or texture: their absence is the style. Small things that keep moving inside a held scene (stars twinkling, dots marching along a dotted line, a lamp flickering, the REC dot) are intended.
- Do report: a pictogram overlapping another so neither reads, text cut off at the frame edge or overlapping other text, text too small to read on a phone, more than one red thing in a scene, a red thing that is not the threat the narration names, a picture that shows something different from the narration, a card that is gone before its text can be read, and a stretch of more than about five seconds where nothing new appears.
script:
Every beat's `visual` is a **pictogram** brief: the small scene it shows (who stands where, what they hold, the one threat in red), or the card it is (a RULE with the thing it forbids, a case card, a phone screen and what it shows, a list of steps). People are faceless pictograms, so a role is "you", "a stranger", "a caller", never a named person.

The narration is a calm, deadpan warning in the second person. Open on the situation as it happens to you ("A stranger sends you a QR code."), then state each rule flatly as a sentence of its own ("Don't scan it."), then say why in one or two short sentences, then what to do instead. A list of rules or steps is the natural shape: number them aloud ("Rule two.") when there are several. Keep sentences short; a new scene starts on most sentences. Say the one thing that is the threat by name, since it is drawn in red. Never write a beat that needs a photograph, a real place or a real person's face: this style has none.

picture.opening: Scene 1 is a picture (a tableau, a camera panel or a phone), on screen from frame 0 with the case-file row already up: the first sentence's situation, never a card.
picture.turn: A glitch tear to a new scene on the first word of a turn or a re-opening, or the threat turning red (redAt) at that moment.
picture.payoff: The RULE card that names what to do or not do, or the scene where the one red threat is plainest.
picture.ending: Hold on the last scene, usually the final RULE or the steps card, to the last frame. No closing card, logo, recap or sign-off after it.

best_for: a security, privacy or scam warning told as rules: if a stranger does X, don't do Y
safety procedures and steps for a bad moment (a stolen phone, a strange call, a knock at night)
internet mysteries and creepy hypotheticals told as a case file
a device, a camera, a stranger or an intruder at the centre of a short warning
avoid_for: a fraud or a scheme told as a story with you inside it that ends on a choice (Case File Story fits it)
how an attack or a protocol works, walked through with generic roles or systems (Stick Explainer acts it out, with System Flow inserts)
a list of unrelated tips, habits or scams with no single threat (Bean Explainer fits it)
dense technical explanation, numbers worked out, or history
a real, named case, company or person
routing.cannot_show: photographs, real places, faces or colour scenes: everything is a white pictogram on black, with one red threat
signals: the script is a list of rules or steps for staying safe
a second-person warning: if X ever happens, do or don't do Y
a stranger, a caller, a link, a code, a camera or an intruder is the danger
one threat can be marked as the only red thing
an incident told as a numbered case
